documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
**INSTRUCTIONS**

**DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN**

- Work Part A first. You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example,

  Doe, Jamie

  A1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. It may not be used in graphing mode. Calculators may not be shared. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas. You may use a ruler or straight edge.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Good luck!

problems.title: A1
problems.statement: A wire of length $l$, radius $r_1$, and resistivity $\rho$ is tightly wound in a single layer into the shape of a solenoid with circular cross section of radius $r_2$. Assume it is an ideal solenoid. A DC voltage $V$ is placed across the ends of the solenoid.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the self inductance of the solenoid?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: If the DC voltage source is replaced with an AC source with rms voltage $\mathrm{V_{rms}}$ and frequency $f$, what is the rms current $I_{\mathrm{rms}}$ through the solenoid?

solution.statement:
a. The magnitude of the magnetic field inside an ideal solenoid is $B = \mu_o nI$

where the number of turns per unit length $n$ is the inverse of the length per turn – the diameter $d$ of the wire.

$$n = \frac{1}{d} = \frac{1}{2r_1}.$$

The total resistance of the wire used to construct the solenoid is

$$R = \rho\frac{l}{A_1} = \rho\frac{l}{\pi r_1^{\,2}}.$$

The current

$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{V\pi r_1^{\,2}}{\rho l}.$$

Combining to find

$$B = \mu_o\left(\frac{1}{2r_1}\right)\left(\frac{V\pi r_1^{\,2}}{\rho l}\right) = \frac{\mu_o \pi V r_1}{2\rho l}$$

b. The self inductance $L$ can be found from

$$LI = N\Phi \qquad \text{(A1-1)}$$

where $N$ is the total number of turns – the length of the wire divided by the circumference of one turn

$$N = \frac{l}{2\pi r_2}$$

and $\Phi$ is the flux through one turn

$$\Phi = B\pi r_2^{\,2} = \mu_o nI\pi r_2^{\,2} = \frac{\mu_o \pi r_2^{\,2}}{2r_1}I$$

combining with (A1-1)

$$L = \frac{N\Phi}{I} = \left(\frac{l}{2\pi r_2}\right)\left(\frac{\mu_o \pi r_2^{\,2}}{2r_1}\right) = \frac{\mu_o r_2 l}{4r_1}$$

c. The inductive impedance is $Z_L = \omega L$. The total impedance of the circuit is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}$

$$I_{rms} = \frac{V_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}} = \frac{V_{rms}}{\sqrt{\left(\frac{\rho l}{\pi r_1^{\,2}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2\pi f\mu_o r_2 l}{4r_1}\right)^2}} = \frac{2r_1V_{rms}}{l\sqrt{\left(\frac{2\rho}{\pi r_1}\right)^2 + \left(\pi f\mu_o r_2\right)^2}}$$

problems.title: A2
problems.statement:
A particle decays into two photons which are both observed to have frequency $f$, one moving at an angle $\theta$ above the positive $x$-axis and the other at an angle of $\theta$ below the positive $x$-axis. See the accompanying diagram. The energy and momentum magnitude of a relativistic particle of mass $m$ and speed $v$ are:

$$E = \frac{mc^2}{\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}} \qquad\qquad p = \frac{mv}{\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}}$$

figures.alt: Decay diagram: a wavy line comes in from the left along the horizontal x-axis and splits at a point into two wavy photon lines with arrowheads, one going up to the right at angle θ above the axis and one going down to the right at angle θ below it; both photons are labelled f and both angles are labelled θ.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the velocity of the original particle.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the rest mass of the original particle.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: What are the frequencies of the decay photons in the rest frame of the particle? What are their directions of travel in this rest frame?

answer.value: Both photons have frequency f' = f sin θ; one travels along the +y-axis and the other along the −y-axis.

solution.statement:
a. The energy and magnitude of the momentum of a photon of frequency $f$ are:

$$E = hf \qquad\qquad p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{hf}{c}.$$

Energy is conserved. Equating the energy of the particle before the decay to the total photon energy after the decay

$$\frac{mc^2}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}} = hf + hf. \qquad \text{(A2-1)}$$

Momentum is conserved. Equating the momentum of the particle before the decay to the sum of the x-components of the photon momentum after the decay

$$\frac{mv}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}} = \frac{hf}{c}\cos\theta + \frac{hf}{c}\cos\theta. \qquad \text{(A2-2)}$$

Dividing (A2-2) by (A2-1)

$$\frac{mv}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}\,\frac{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}{mc^2} = \frac{(2hf/c)\cos\theta}{2hf}$$

Or

$$\frac{v}{c^2} = \frac{\cos\theta}{c}$$

$$v = c\cos\theta \quad \text{in the positive } x\text{-direction} \qquad \text{(A2-3)}$$

b. Solving (A2-1) for $mc^2$

$$mc^2 = 2hf\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}$$

and substituting in (A2-3)

$$mc^2 = 2hf\sqrt{1-(c\cos\theta/c)^2} = 2hf\sqrt{1-(\cos\theta)^2} = 2hf\sin\theta$$

$$m = \frac{2hf}{c^2}\sin\theta \qquad \text{(A2-4)}$$

c. In this frame, the particle has zero momentum, so the momentum of the final photons must be equal and opposite – one along the +$y$-axis, the other along the -$y$-axis. If each photon’s momentum has the same magnitude, the photons must have the same frequency $f'$.

In this frame the particles energy is $mc^2$. Applying energy conservation

$$mc^2 = 2hf'.$$

Solving for $f'$ and substituting in (A2-4)

$$f' = \frac{mc^2}{2h} = \left(\frac{2hf}{c^2}\sin\theta\right)\frac{c^2}{2h} = f\sin\theta$$

problems.title: A3
problems.statement: Fundamental quanta of length, time, and mass are the Planck length $\lambda_{\mathrm{P}}$, the Planck time $t_{\mathrm{P}}$, and the Planck mass $m_{\mathrm{P}}$. Use the fact that they depend only on the Newton’s gravitational constant $G$, Planck’s constant $h$, and speed of light in a vacuum $c$ and no other constant to derive expressions for them and then calculate their numerical values.

solution.statement:
The Planck length $\lambda_{\mathrm{P}}$, the Planck time $t_{\mathrm{P}}$, and the Planck mass $m_{\mathrm{P}}$ depend only on the Newton’s gravitational constant $G$, Planck’s constant $h$, and speed of light in a vacuum $c$ and no other constant. Use dimensional analysis to obtain the equations. Let

[T] represent the dimension of time

[L] represent the dimension of length

[M] represent the dimension of mass

Since $G$ has units $\mathrm{N{\bullet}m^2/kg^2 = (kg{\bullet}m/s^2)\ m^2/kg^2 = m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}$ its dimensions are $[L]^3[M]^{-1}[T]^{-2}$ for $G$

$h$ has units $\mathrm{J\ s = (kg{\bullet}m^2/s^2)s = m^2kg^1s^{-1}}$ its dimensions are $[L]^2[M]^1[T]^{-1}$ for $h$

$c$ has units $\mathrm{m/s = m^1s^{-1}}$ its dimensions are $[L]^1[M]^0[T]^{-1}$ for $c$

Let

$$\lambda_p = G^ah^bc^d.$$

Then analyzing the dimensions

$$[L]^1[M]^0[T]^0 = [L]^{3a}[M]^{-a}[T]^{-2a}[L]^{2b}[M]^{b}[T]^{-b}[L]^{d}[M]^0[T]^{-d} = [L]^{3a+2b+d}[M]^{-a+b}[T]^{-2a-b-d}.$$

Equating exponents of [L] $\quad 1 = 3a+2b+d$

Equating exponents of [M] $\quad 0 = -a+b$

Equating exponents of [T] $\quad 0 = -2a-b-d$

Solving these equations $\quad b = a$ and $d = -3a$ then $1 = 3a + 2a - 3a = 2a$

So $a = 1/2$, $b = 1/2$, and $d = -3/2$ and

$$\lambda_p = G^{1/2}h^{1/2}c^{-3/2} = \left(\frac{Gh}{c^3}\right)^{1/2} = \left(\frac{\left(6.67\times10^{-11}\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}\right)\left(6.63\times10^{-34}\mathrm{J\cdot s}\right)}{\left(3.0\times10^{8}\mathrm{m/s}\right)^3}\right)^{1/2} = 4.05\times10^{-35}\mathrm{m}$$

Let

$$t_p = G^ah^bc^d.$$

Then analyzing the dimensions

$$[L]^0[M]^0[T]^1 = [L]^{3a+2b+d}[M]^{-a+b}[T]^{-2a-b-d}.$$

Equating exponents of [L] $\quad 0 = 3a+2b+d$

Equating exponents of [M] $\quad 0 = -a+b$

Equating exponents of [T] $\quad 1 = -2a-b-d$

Solving these equations $\quad b = a$, $d = -5a$, and $1 = -2a - a + 5a = 2a$

So $a = 1/2$, $b = 1/2m$ and $d = -5/2$

$$t_p = G^{1/2}h^{1/2}c^{-5/2} = \left(\frac{Gh}{c^5}\right)^{1/2} = \left(\frac{\left(6.67\times10^{-11}\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}\right)\left(6.63\times10^{-34}\mathrm{J\cdot s}\right)}{\left(3.0\times10^{8}\mathrm{m/s}\right)^5}\right)^{1/2} = 1.35\times10^{-43}\mathrm{s}$$

Let

$$m_p = G^ah^bc^d.$$

Then analyzing the dimensions

$$[L]^0[M]^1[T]^0 = [L]^{3a+2b+d}[M]^{-a+b}[T]^{-2a-b-d}.$$

Equating exponents of [L] $\quad 0 = 3a+2b+d$

Equating exponents of [M] $\quad 1 = -a+b$

Equating exponents of [T] $\quad 0 = -2a-b-d$

Solving these equations $\quad a = -1/2$, $b = 1/2$, and $d = 1/2$

$$m_p = G^{-1/2}h^{1/2}c^{1/2} = \left(\frac{hc}{G}\right)^{1/2} = \left(\frac{\left(6.63\times10^{-34}\mathrm{J\cdot s}\right)\left(3.0\times10^{8}\mathrm{m/s}\right)}{\left(6.67\times10^{-11}\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}\right)}\right)^{1/2} = 5.46\times10^{-8}\mathrm{kg}$$

problems.title: A4
problems.statement: A 0.75-m rod has a uniform linear mass density of $\lambda$. A small mass $m$ with negligible volume is attached to one end of the rod. The rod with the attached mass is placed in a container of unknown fluid and after oscillating briefly comes to rest in its equilibrium position. At equilibrium it floats vertically (mass $m$ end down) with 2/3 of its length submerged. If the rod were fully submerged it would displace $7.5\ \mathrm{x}10^{-4}$ kg of fluid.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the maximum value that the mass $m$ can have?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the minimum value that the mass $m$ can have?

answer.note: Strict bound: m > 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ kg (stable equilibrium requires λL < 2m).

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Sketch a graph that shows the values of $\lambda$ as a function of $m$.

answer.value: λ = (5.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg − m)/L: a straight line with negative slope from λ = 0.44 g/m at m = 0.17 g to λ = 0 at m = 0.50 g.

solution.statement:
a. Let $L = 0.75$ m, the length of the rod.

$\rho$ = the density of the unknown fluid

$V$ = the total volume of the rod

$\lambda L$ = mass of the rod

Since if the rod were fully submerged it would displaced $7.5\times10^{-4}$ kgof fluid, $\quad 7.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} = \rho V$

In the present case the rod is only 2/3 submerged so The buoyant force acting on the rod is

$$B = W_{fl\ dis} = \rho\left(\tfrac{2}{3}V\right)g = \tfrac{2}{3}\left(7.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg}\right)g = \left(5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg}\right)g$$

Since the system is in equilibrium the buoyant force balances the total weight force.

$$\left(5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg}\right)g = mg + \lambda Lg$$

or

$$5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} = m + \lambda L. \qquad \text{(A4-1)}$$

Since $\lambda$ cannot be negative the largest value m can have is $\quad 5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} \ge m$.

b. The system oscillates and comes to rest. It must be in stable equilibrium. For this to occur the center of gravity must be below the center of buoyancy. The fluid is uniform. The center of buoyancy is at the mid point of the submerged length. Measuring distances from the bottom end of the rod, the location of the center of buoyancy is

$$y_{cb} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{2}{3}L\right) = \tfrac{1}{3}L.$$

Mass $m$ is located at $y = 0$. The center of gravity of the rod is at $L/2$. The combined center of gravity of the system $y_{cg}$ is

$$y_{cg}\sum m_ig = \sum y_im_ig$$

$$y_{cg}(m + \lambda L)g = 0mg + (L/2)(\lambda L)g$$

$$y_{cg} = \frac{\lambda L^2}{2(m + \lambda L)}$$

Requiring the center of gravity to be below the center of buoyancy

$$y_{cg} < y_{cb}$$

$$\frac{\lambda L^2}{2(m + \lambda L)} < \frac{1}{3}L$$

$$3\lambda L < 2(m + \lambda L)$$

or

$$\lambda L < 2m$$

Combining this with (A4-1)

$$5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} < m + 2m$$

Or

$$m > \frac{1}{3}\left(5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg}\right) = 1.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg}$$

c. Solving (A4-1) for $\lambda$

$$\lambda = \frac{5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} - m}{L} = \frac{0.5\ \mathrm{grams} - m}{0.75\ \mathrm{m}}.$$

At its minimum value $m_{min} = 1.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} = 0.17$ grams, $\lambda = 0.44$ grams / m

At its maximum value $m_{max} = 5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg} = 0.50$ grams, $\lambda = 0$.

The graph is a straight line with negative slope between these two points.

figures.alt: Graph of λ in g/m (vertical axis) against m in g (horizontal axis): a straight line falling from λ = 0.44 at m = 0.17 to λ = 0 at m = 0.500. Axis labels: “λ in g/m”, “m in g”; tick labels 0.44, 0.17, 0.500.

problems.title: B1
problems.statement: A thin semicircular hoop of radius $R$ and mass $m$ rocks back and forth without slipping on a rough surface. The center-of-mass of this hoop lies a distance $2R/\pi$ below its center of curvature when it is in its equilibrium position. See diagrams above.

figures.alt: Two diagrams of a semicircular hoop resting on a horizontal line. Left: the hoop in equilibrium, with a radius arrow labelled R from the center of curvature to the hoop and a vertical arrow labelled 2R/π from the center of curvature down to a cross marked cm. Right: the hoop tilted, touching the line at a point below the center of curvature, with the radius arrow R, a vertical line from the center of curvature to the contact point, and a tilted arrow 2R/π to the cross marked cm.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the semicircular hoop’s moment of inertia about its center of mass?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find $T_{\mathrm{no\ slip}}$ the period of oscillation for small amplitude oscillations. Ignore all terms higher than first order in the oscillation angle $\theta$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: The hoop now undergoes oscillations on a frictionless surface with the period of oscillation $T_{\mathrm{slip}}$. Ignore all terms higher than first order in the oscillation angle $\theta$. Find the ratio of $T_{\mathrm{slip}}$ to $T_{\mathrm{no\ slip}}$.

solution.statement:
(10) a. The semicircular hoop’s moment of inertia about its center is $I = mR^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem to find the moment of inertia about the center of mass $I_{cm}$

$$I = I_{cm} + mh^2$$

where $h$ is the perpendicular distance between an axis through the center of mass and a parallel axis through an arbitrary point.

In this case

$$h = \frac{2R}{\pi}$$

$$I_{cm} = I - mh^2 = mR^2 - m\left(\frac{2R}{\pi}\right)^2 = mR^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}\right)$$

(20) b. Finding the moment of inertia about the stationary point, the point where the hoop is in contact with the surface.

$$I = I_{cm} + mL^2 = mR^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}\right) + mL^2.$$

Using the Law of cosines to find $L$

$$L^2 = R^2 + \left(\frac{2R}{\pi}\right)^2 - \frac{4R^2}{\pi}\cos\theta.$$

Substituting into the expression for $I$

$$I = mR^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}\right) + m\left(R^2 + \left(\frac{2R}{\pi}\right)^2 - \frac{4R^2}{\pi}\cos\theta\right)$$

$$I = mR^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2} + 1 + \frac{4}{\pi^2} - \frac{4}{\pi}\cos\theta\right) = mR^2\left(2 - \frac{4}{\pi}\cos\theta\right).$$

For small amplitude oscillations (keeping only terms through first order in $\theta$

$$\cos\theta \approx 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad I \approx 2mR^2\left(1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\right).$$

The restoring torque about the stationary point is

$$\tau = -mgd = -mg\left(\frac{2R}{\pi}\right)\sin\theta \approx -\frac{2mgR}{\pi}\theta,$$

where the small angle approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ has been used.

Combining the last two equations in $\tau = I\alpha$,

yields

$$-\frac{2mgR}{\pi}\theta \approx 2mR^2\left(1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\right)\alpha.$$

Comparing this with the defining equation of simple harmonic motion $-\omega^2x = a$, gives an expression for $\omega^2$.

$$\omega^2 = \frac{2mgR}{\pi 2mR^2\left(1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\right)} = \frac{g}{R\pi\left(1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\right)} = \frac{g}{R(\pi - 2)}.$$

For the period $T_{no\ slip}$

$$T_{no\ slip} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{g}{R(\pi - 2)}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R(\pi - 2)}{g}}$$

(20) c. There is no horizontal force. The center of mass does not move from side to side. The y-coordinate of the center of mass is

$$y = R - \frac{2R}{\pi}\cos\theta = R - \frac{2R}{\pi}\left(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} + \ldots\right) \approx R - \frac{2R}{\pi}$$

including only terms through first order in $\theta$. To this approximation, the vertical position of the center of mass is constant and its acceleration is zero as well. Thus

$$\sum F_y = N - mg = ma_y \approx 0$$

or

$$N \approx mg.$$

Taking torques about the center of mass

$$\tau = -Nd = -N\frac{2R}{\pi}\sin\theta \approx -\frac{2mgR}{\pi}\theta$$

where we have once again used the small angle approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$.

$$\tau = I_{cm}\alpha$$

$$-\frac{2mgR}{\pi}\theta \approx mR^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}\right)\alpha$$

Comparing this with the defining equation of simple harmonic motion $-\omega^2x = a$, gives an expression for $\omega^2$.

$$\omega^2 = \frac{2mgR}{\pi mR^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}\right)} = \frac{2g}{R\pi\left(1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}\right)} = \frac{2g\pi}{R\left(\pi^2 - 4\right)}.$$

For the period $T_{slip}$

$$T_{slip} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{2g\pi}{R\left(\pi^2 - 4\right)}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R\left(\pi^2 - 4\right)}{2g\pi}}.$$

The ratio of periods is

$$\frac{T_{slip}}{T_{no\ slip}} = \frac{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R\left(\pi^2 - 4\right)}{2g\pi}}}{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R(\pi - 2)}{g}}} = \sqrt{\frac{R\left(\pi^2 - 4\right)g}{2g\pi R(\pi - 2)}} = \sqrt{\frac{(\pi - 2)(\pi + 2)}{2\pi(\pi - 2)}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi + 2}{2\pi}}$$

figures.alt: Tilted semicircular hoop on a horizontal surface: a vertical line from the center of curvature to the contact point, a line of length 2R/π at angle θ from the vertical to the center of mass (cm), the weight arrow mg at the cm, the horizontal lever arm d, the radius R and the distance L from the cm to the contact point.

Tilted semicircular hoop on a frictionless surface: the line of length 2R/π at angle θ from the vertical to the center of mass (cm), the weight arrow mg, the normal force N pointing up at the contact point, the lever arm d and the radius R.

problems.title: B2
problems.statement: A total charge $+Q$ is uniformly distributed throughout a sphere of radius $R$. Charge is removed from a spherical hole of radius $R/2$ centered on the $z = R/2$ point of the z-axis and concentrated into a point charge $q$ which is placed at the center of the hole. See Fig. B1-1 above.

figures.caption: Figure B2-1
figures.alt: Cross-section in the x–z plane of a shaded sphere of radius R centered at the origin, with an unshaded spherical hole of radius R/2 touching the top of the sphere; a point charge q sits at the center of the hole. Arrows mark the radii R and R/2; axes x (right) and z (up).

figures.caption: Figure B2-2
figures.alt: The same cross-section as Figure B2-1 but without the point charge: a shaded sphere of radius R with an empty spherical hole of radius R/2 touching the top; arrows mark R and R/2; axes x and z.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the charge $q$ in terms of $Q$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the electric field at all points along the $x$-axis.

answer.value: For |x| > R: E = kQ/R² (as printed); for |x| < R: E = kQ|x|/R³; in a direction out from the origin.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: The charge $q$ is now removed, leaving the charge distribution seen in Fig. B2-2 above. Find the electric field at all points along the $z$-axis.

answer.value: |z| > R: E = kQ/z² − kQ/(8(z − R/2)²); −R < z < 0: E = kQ|z|/R³ − kQ/(8(z − R/2)²); 0 < z < R: E = kQ/(2R²); out from the origin.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Find the electrostatic potential at an arbitrary point $x$, $y$, $z$ outside the sphere of radius $R$ as shown in Fig. B2-2 above. Assume the potential vanishes at an infinite distance from the charges.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement:
Very far from the charge distribution, the electrostatic potential may be written in the following form

$$V = k\left(\frac{a}{r} + \frac{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{r}}{r^3} + \ldots\right)$$

where $r$ is the distance from the origin at the center of the large sphere. Using your result from part d) above, determine the constant $a$ and the constant vector $\vec{b}$. ($\vec{b}$ is called the electric dipole moment.)

parts.label: f.
parts.statement: Interpret $a$ and $\vec{b}$ in terms of a set of discrete charges and their locations.

answer.value: A point charge of 7Q/8 at the origin and a dipole consisting of −Q/8 at (0, 0, R/2) and +Q/8 at the origin.

solution.statement:
(5) a. If the charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed, the charge density is

$$\rho = \frac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}.$$

The charge in a sphere of radius $R/2$ is

$$q = \rho\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}\rho\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}\frac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}Q.$$

(10) b. The $x$-axis is totally outside the cavity. By Gauss’s Law the field outside a spherical symmetric charge distribution of radius $R/2$ centered on $z = R/2$ is the same as that due to point charge at the center with the same total charge. So on the $x$-axis the field is the same as that due to uniform charge distribution of total charge $Q$ and radius $R$.

From Gauss’s Law for a spherically symmetric charge distribution

$$E = k\frac{Q_{enc}}{R^2}$$

where $k$ is Coulomb’s constant and $Q_{enc}$ is the total charge enclosed by a Gaussian sphere of radius $R$.

Outside the sphere $\quad Q_{enc} = Q$

For $|x| > R$ $\quad E = k\dfrac{Q}{R^2}$ $\quad$ in a direction out from the origin.

Inside the sphere $\quad Q_{enc} = \rho\tfrac{4}{3}\pi|x|^3 = \dfrac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}\tfrac{4}{3}\pi|x|^3 = \dfrac{Q|x|^3}{R^3}$

For $|x| < R$ $\quad E = k\dfrac{1}{x^2}\dfrac{Q|x|^3}{R^3} = k\dfrac{Q|x|}{R^3}$ $\quad$ in a direction out from the origin.

(10) c. The total field can be considered the sum of two terms. That due to:

a sphere of radius $R$ centered on the origin with uniformly distributed total charge $+Q$.

a sphere of radius $R/2$ centered on $z = R/2$ with uniformly distributed total charge $-Q/8$.

Outside the large sphere both fields are equal to those due to point charges at their centers.

For $|z| > R$ $\quad E = k\dfrac{Q}{z^2} - k\dfrac{Q}{8(z - R/2)^2}$ $\quad$ out from the origin.

Inside the large sphere but outside the cavity, treat the cavity as a point charge at its center and the sphere as an extended distribution

For $-R < z < 0$ $\quad E = k\dfrac{Q|z|}{R^3} - k\dfrac{Q}{8(z - R/2)^2}$ $\quad$ out from the origin.

Inside the cavity, treat both the sphere and cavities as extended charge distributions.

$0 < z < R/2$ $\quad E = k\dfrac{Qz}{R^3} + k\dfrac{Q(R/2 - z)}{8(R/2)^3} = k\dfrac{Qz}{R^3} + k\dfrac{Q(R/2 - z)}{R^3} = k\dfrac{Q}{2R^2}$ $\quad$ out from the origin.

$R/2 < z < R$ $\quad E = k\dfrac{Qz}{R^3} - k\dfrac{Q(z - R/2)}{8(R/2)^3} = k\dfrac{Qz}{R^3} + k\dfrac{Q(R/2 - z)}{R^3} = k\dfrac{Q}{2R^2}$ $\quad$ out from the origin.

(10) d. Outside the sphere, the electrostatic potential is the same as that due to a point charge of $+Q$ at the origin and a point charge of $-Q/8$ at $x = 0$, $y = 0$, $z = R/2$.

Writing the distance from the origin as $\quad r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$

and the distance from at $x = 0$, $y = 0$, $z = R/2$. as $\quad r' = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + (z - R/2)^2}$.

The potential is

$$V = k\frac{Q}{r} - k\frac{q}{r'} = k\frac{Q}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}} - k\frac{Q}{8\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + (z - R/2)^2}}$$

(10) e. In order to get the electrostatic potential in the form shown, expand $r'$ in a binomial series.

$$r' = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + (z - R/2)^2} = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - zR + R^2/4} = \sqrt{r^2 - zR + R^2/4} = r\sqrt{1 - \frac{zR}{r^2} + \frac{R^2}{4r^2}}$$

$$V = k\frac{Q}{r} - k\frac{q}{r'} = k\frac{Q}{r} - k\frac{Q}{8r\sqrt{1 - \frac{zR}{r^2} + \frac{R^2}{4r^2}}} \approx k\frac{Q}{r} - k\frac{Q}{8r}\left(1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{zR}{r^2} - \frac{1}{2}\frac{R^2}{4r^2} + \ldots\right) \approx k\left(\frac{7Q}{8r} - \frac{QzR}{16r^3} + \ldots\right)$$

Only terms of order $\dfrac{1}{r}$ and of order $\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}^2}$ $\left(\text{such as } \dfrac{z}{r^3}\right)$ have been retained.

Comparing to the expression for $V$ given in 2Be $\quad a = \tfrac{7}{8}Q$

And with $z = \vec{r}\cdot\hat{k}$ $\quad \vec{b}\cdot\vec{r} = -\dfrac{QzR}{16} = -\dfrac{Q\left(\vec{r}\cdot\hat{k}\right)R}{16}.$

Which gives $\quad \vec{b} = -\dfrac{QR}{16}\hat{k}$

(5) f. A point charge of $\frac{7}{8}Q$ at the origin and a dipole consisting of $-\frac{1}{8}Q$ at (0, 0, $R/2$) and $+\frac{1}{8}Q$ at the origin.
